questions.q: What is the exact amount of money Hari Singh steals from Anil, and where does Anil keep it?
questions.a: Hari steals 600 rupees, which Anil keeps under the mattress. A wrong answer (e.g., "500 rupees" or "from Anil's pocket") reveals the student has not read the text closely and relies on vague memory — a critical error in board exams where textual precision earns marks.

questions.q: Explain in your own words why Hari hesitates at the railway station instead of boarding the train to Lucknow.
questions.a: Hari hesitates because Anil's trust and the prospect of learning to write create a moral conflict; he realizes stealing would betray the only person who treated him with kindness and destroy his chance at a respectable future. A wrong answer focusing only on "fear of getting caught" or "the rain" misses the psychological depth — the conflict is internal, not external.

questions.q: Apply the concept of "turning point" to this scene: Identify the single sentence in the text that marks the climax of Hari's internal conflict and justify your choice.
questions.a: The sentence "I had forgotten about them in the excitement of the theft" (referring to the notes getting wet) is the climax because it forces Hari to physically confront the consequences of his act — the ruined notes make the theft pointless, mirroring his internal realization that the theft has ruined his self-respect. A wrong answer picking a descriptive line (e.g., "The train had not yet arrived") shows inability to distinguish plot events from character-defining moments.

questions.q: Analyze how the rain functions as a literary device in this scene. Compare its literal and symbolic roles.
questions.a: Literally, the rain soaks Hari and the stolen notes, making the money unusable and giving him a practical reason to return. Symbolically, it represents purification — washing away his identity as a thief and marking his rebirth as an honest learner. A wrong answer treating rain only as "bad weather" or only as "symbol of sadness" fails to integrate both levels, losing marks for incomplete analysis.

questions.q: Evaluate this statement: "Hari returns the money only because the notes are wet; if they had stayed dry, he would have left on the train." Defend your position with textual evidence.
questions.a: The statement is false. Before the rain, Hari already thinks, "I knew I would not be able to cook his meals, run to the bazaar, learn to write whole sentences..." — showing his conscience has already weighed the loss of education against the gain of money. The rain accelerates the decision but doesn't cause it. A wrong answer agreeing with the statement ignores Hari's earlier reflective thoughts, a common board-exam trap where students confuse catalyst with cause.

questions.q: Create a diary entry from Hari's perspective that night, capturing his internal debate in first person. Use at least three sensory details from the text (e.g., sound of rain, feel of wet notes, smell of the station).
questions.a: A strong entry will show the debate: "The 600 rupees feel heavy in my pocket, not light like before. The rain hammers the tin roof — each drop says 'go back.' The notes stick together, wet and useless, like my old life. But Anil's face when he taught me 'H-a-r-i'... I can't steal that future." A poor entry narrates events without internal conflict or sensory details, showing the student cannot inhabit the character's perspective — a skill needed for creative writing questions.
